prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: That, Kenji, Takezo

outputs.L1:
That boy, the champion breath-holder, Kenji Takezo, lost his title this year to Mack Stanton, a retired truck driver new to the area.

The contest was held in the town swimming pool. Thirty-five participants inhaled deeply all at once and submerged themselves in the depths. It went on into twilight. One by one, each person came up sucking air.

Kenji was the town favorite. We wanted him to win again. He had trained so hard; it was the only real talent he had, other than surfing and making trouble. When he surfaced second to last, gulping the night air and then vomiting water, we were disappointed. He had been doing so well. He had his lucky twenty-pound brick cradled in his lap. It kept him down.

But that trucker, Mack, was too good. He read comic books aloud underwater. We watched from the bleachers as his laughter burst above him. Kenji saw this, too. He had never had anybody read to him, not even his mother, and he wanted to hear what was being read—what his opponent found so funny.
outputs.L2:
Kenji Takezo, the boy known for holding his breath longer than anyone else, was beaten this year and lost his championship. The winner was Mack Stanton, a retired trucker who had only recently moved to town.

The competition took place at the municipal pool. Thirty-five contestants drew in huge breaths together and sank beneath the water. The event stretched on until dusk. Gradually, they rose one after another, gasping for air.

Everyone in town had expected Kenji to win. We were rooting for him to keep his title. He had practiced relentlessly; breath-holding was one of the few things he was truly good at, besides surfing and causing problems.

When he finally broke the surface as the next-to-last person, swallowing the dark air and then throwing up pool water, we felt let down. He had been doing so well. His lucky twenty-pound brick had rested in his lap, weighing him securely underwater.

But Mack, the truck driver, was better. Beneath the surface, he read comic books out loud. From the bleachers, we could see his laughter bubbling upward.

Kenji noticed it too. No one had ever read aloud to him, not even his own mother, and he longed to know the words Mack was reading and what was making his rival laugh.
outputs.L3:
Kenji Takezo had long been known as the town’s champion breath holder. For years, no one had been able to stay underwater longer than he could, and many people considered him unbeatable. He was a familiar figure around town, famous not only for his breath-holding talent but also for his surfing, his intense training, and his habit of getting into trouble. Because of this reputation, most of the townspeople expected him to win again.

The competition took place at the town swimming pool, where thirty-five participants gathered to test their endurance. One by one, they slipped beneath the surface and tried to remain underwater for as long as possible. As the minutes passed, contestants began popping back up for air. The crowd watched eagerly as the number of competitors grew smaller and smaller, until only two remained: Kenji Takezo and Mack Stanton.

Mack was a retired truck driver who had only recently moved to the area. Since he was new in town, few people knew much about him, and almost no one expected him to challenge Kenji. Still, Mack seemed calm and unbothered as the contest went on. Kenji, meanwhile, relied on every trick he knew. He even used his lucky twenty-pound brick, which helped weigh him down and keep him underwater. The crowd waited for their champion to outlast Mack as he always had outlasted everyone else.

But this time, Kenji did not win. To the disappointment of the spectators, he surfaced second to last, gasping for air while Mack remained underwater. The town favorite had lost his title.

What made Mack’s victory even stranger was the way he won. Instead of simply holding his breath in silence, Mack stayed calm by reading comic books aloud underwater. This fascinated Kenji. He had never had anyone read to him before, and Mack’s odd method made him curious. Although Kenji had lost the championship, he found himself interested in the retired truck driver who had beaten him—and in the stories Mack had been reading beneath the water.
outputs.L4:
Every summer, when the heat settled over the town like a wool blanket and the public pool became the center of everyone’s world, the recreation committee held its strangest and most beloved event: the annual breath-holding contest.

It was not a race, exactly, and not a feat of strength. There were no lanes, no starting pistol, no cheering during the crucial moments. Contestants simply climbed into the deep end, took one last breath, and sank beneath the surface. Whoever remained underwater the longest was declared the winner.

For years, that winner had been Kenji Takezo.

Kenji was not a large man, nor a loud one. He worked at the hardware store on Main Street and lived alone in a small apartment above the laundromat. But in the pool, he had the seriousness of an athlete and the calm of a monk. He trained for the contest weeks in advance, timing his breathing, practicing stillness, walking long distances without speaking to anyone. Children whispered about him as if he had gills. Adults clapped him on the back and called him “champ.” Kenji pretended not to enjoy the attention, but he did. It was the one day each year when the whole town looked at him and saw someone remarkable.

His method was famous. While other contestants kicked and drifted, wasting strength, Kenji used a heavy red brick borrowed from the maintenance shed. He held it against his chest and let it carry him down to the tiled floor of the pool, where he sat cross-legged like a statue. The brick kept him anchored. His eyes remained closed. His body barely moved. Above him, the crowd became a blur of legs, sun hats, and distorted faces peering through blue water.

This year, everyone expected Kenji to win again.

Then Mack Stanton arrived.

Mack was new in town, a broad-shouldered man with sandy hair, a crooked smile, and a habit of appearing at events as though he had wandered into them by accident. No one knew much about him except that he rented the old yellow house near the train tracks and worked nights somewhere outside town. When he signed up for the contest, people laughed politely, assuming he had no idea what he was entering.

Kenji noticed him immediately.

Mack did not stretch. He did not test his lungs or ask about the rules. He simply sat on the edge of the pool with a stack of comic books sealed in a plastic sleeve beside him. When someone asked what they were for, Mack shrugged and said, “Something to pass the time.”

The contestants lined up at the deep end shortly after noon. The sun flashed on the water. Children crowded the fence. The mayor, wearing a whistle and a straw hat, explained the rules for the benefit of anyone who had somehow missed them in previous years.

“No air tanks. No tricks. No coming up and going back down. Once your head breaks the surface, you’re out.”

Kenji listened with his usual solemn expression. His brick waited at his feet.

At the whistle, everyone inhaled.

Then they went under.

At first, the contest followed its familiar pattern. The youngest contestants gave up within twenty seconds, bursting upward with panicked laughter. A high school swimmer lasted nearly a minute, then surfaced red-faced and gasping. Two men from the fire department tried to outdo each other and failed almost together, slapping the water as they came up.

Below them, Kenji had already settled into position.

He sat on the pool floor, brick clutched against his ribs, and emptied himself of movement. He thought of nothing. That was the discipline. Thought burned oxygen. Want burned oxygen. Fear burned oxygen. Kenji had trained himself to become a sealed room.

But across from him, Mack Stanton was doing something impossible.

Mack had sunk to the bottom without a brick. He sat with his back against the pool wall, legs stretched out, perfectly relaxed. In his hands was one of the comic books, opened inside a clear waterproof folder. His cheeks were puffed slightly, and bubbles leaked from his mouth as he read.

At first Kenji assumed he was hallucinating.

Then he heard it.

The sound was warped by the water, thick and ridiculous, but unmistakable. Mack was speaking. Not clearly, not normally, but speaking all the same, releasing words in a slow, bubbling stream.

“Captain Meteor raised his silver fist…”

Tiny bubbles rose past his face.

“…and vowed that the Moon Pirates would never conquer Earth…”

Kenji’s eyes widened.

Above the surface, the spectators had fallen into baffled silence. They could not hear the words as Kenji could, but they could see Mack turning the pages. They could see him reading calmly, as if seated in a barber shop waiting for a haircut.

Kenji tightened his grip on the brick.

This was foolish, he told himself. Speaking underwater meant losing air. Mack would be up any second. No one could waste breath like that and still win.

But Mack did not come up.

He read on.

Kenji shut his eyes again and tried to return to his training. He counted heartbeats. He slowed his body. He imagined himself as stone, as iron, as something heavy and patient. But the words kept reaching him through the water.

“The villain laughed from his crystal tower…”

A page turned.

“…while beneath the city, the forgotten machine began to wake.”

Kenji felt the first pang in his chest.

It was not yet pain. It was a message from the body, a polite reminder. Air would be needed soon. He had ignored this message many times before. He could ignore it now.

Yet something was different.

Mack’s voice, bubbling and broken, made the silence inside Kenji seem suddenly enormous. For years, Kenji had won by needing nothing. He had made an art of deprivation. He had taught himself to close every door: no curiosity, no fear, no desire, no movement toward the world. The brick in his arms was not just a tool; it was a promise. Stay down. Stay still. Want less.

But Mack wanted to know what happened next.

That was the absurdity of it. Mack was not enduring the water; he was occupying it. He was not fighting the lack of air; he was spending what little he had on a story.

Kenji opened his eyes again.

Mack glanced up from the comic and smiled at him.

It was not a cruel smile. That made it worse. It was friendly, almost inviting, as though Mack were sharing a secret: there are better reasons to hold your breath than winning.

Kenji’s chest tightened. His throat pulsed. The blue water shimmered around him. Above, the crowd leaned closer, their faces stretched and strange.

He tried to think of victory, of applause, of the mayor raising his hand. He tried to think of the children chanting his name. But another thought entered, small and sharp: What happens to Captain Meteor?

The question startled him.

Kenji had not read a comic book since he was a boy. He remembered lying on his stomach in his parents’ kitchen, chin in his hands, devouring bright pages full of impossible machines and doomed planets. He remembered being curious before he learned to be disciplined. He remembered wanting things without measuring the cost.

Mack turned another page.

Kenji’s lungs clenched.

The brick grew heavier. For the first time, it seemed less like an anchor than a burden. His fingers loosened. The red block slipped from his hands and struck the pool floor with a dull, muted thud.

A gasp moved through the crowd above, though Kenji heard it only as a trembling in the water.

He kicked once.

Then again.

His head broke the surface, and the world rushed back in: sunlight, shouting, chlorine, heat, breath. Kenji inhaled violently, bending forward, water streaming from his hair and face. The crowd applauded out of habit, then quieted, unsure whether to celebrate or mourn.

Below him, Mack Stanton remained underwater.

He finished the page.

Then, with unhurried grace, he closed the comic book, tucked it under one arm, and pushed off from the wall. When he surfaced, he took a modest breath, wiped his eyes, and looked around as if surprised to find so many people watching.

The mayor blew the whistle.

“Mack Stanton wins!”

The pool erupted. Children cheered. Adults laughed in disbelief. Someone shouted, “He was reading!” as though no one else had noticed.

Mack climbed out of the pool and accepted a towel. Kenji stayed in the water, one hand on the edge, still breathing hard.

After a moment, Mack crouched beside him.

“Good contest,” he said.

Kenji looked up. “How did you do that?”

Mack smiled. “I wanted to finish the issue.”

Kenji almost laughed, but the sound caught in his throat. He looked down through the water at the brick resting on the pool floor. It seemed smaller now, ordinary and sad.

“What happens?” Kenji asked.

Mack tilted his head. “In the comic?”

Kenji nodded.

Mack handed him the waterproof folder. “You can borrow it.”

The crowd had already begun to drift toward the refreshment table, retelling the story in louder and less accurate versions. By evening, people would say Mack had read an entire novel underwater. By next summer, they would claim he had recited Shakespeare. Kenji knew how town legends worked. He had been one.

But for the moment, he remained in the pool, holding the comic book against the wet concrete edge.

He had lost the contest. Everyone had seen it. The old champion had risen first, defeated not by stronger lungs or better training, but by a man who had brought curiosity into a place where Kenji had only ever brought denial.

And yet, as Kenji opened the comic to the page Mack had marked, he felt something unfamiliar beneath his embarrassment.

Not victory.

Not exactly happiness.

A hunger.

He wanted to know what happened next.
outputs.L5:
That morning, Kenji found an old wooden charm tucked beneath the floorboards of his grandfather’s house. The name “Takezo” was carved into its surface, the letters worn smooth by time. No one in the family had spoken of Takezo for years, yet Kenji felt as if the charm had been waiting for him.

Curious, he carried it to the garden, where the first light of dawn touched the stones and moss. As he held the charm, he remembered the stories his grandmother used to tell: Takezo had been a traveler, a man who crossed mountains and rivers in search of wisdom. He believed that every person must find a path of their own, even if it began with a single uncertain step.

That thought stayed with Kenji. He had been afraid to leave the village, afraid to chase the dreams that pulled at his heart. But with Takezo’s charm in his hand, he felt a quiet courage growing inside him.

By sunset, Kenji had packed a small bag. He bowed to the house, slipped the charm into his pocket, and stepped onto the road. That was the beginning of his journey.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a small-town breath-holding contest where the reigning teenage champion loses to an unlikely newcomer.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon the whole town gathered in the drained swimming pool, because the lake had begun dreaming again and could not be trusted.

They came with lemonade, stopwatches, folding chairs, the church bell polished to a yellow glare. The barber brought a comb for luck. The mayor wore his sash made of minnows. Above us the sky held its own breath, blue-faced and stubborn.

Caleb June, seventeen, reigning champion of three summers, stood barefoot on the diving board like a prince of lungs. He had once stayed under so long that the water forgot his name. Girls wrote it on their wrists. Boys practiced fainting behind the feed store. His mother kept his trophies dusted with a pigeon feather.

Then the newcomer arrived: Mrs. Pruitt’s scarecrow from the bean field, walking on two broomsticks, wearing a hat full of thunderstorms. Nobody knew who had invited him. He smelled of straw, rain, and things kept secret in barns. A crow sat on his shoulder and read the rules aloud in a judge’s voice.

The contest began.

Caleb inhaled first. The sound drew curtains inward all along Main Street. Dogs slid under porches. The balloons tied to the hardware store flattened into little red coins. He filled himself until his ribs shone like a picket fence around a trapped moon.

The scarecrow did nothing.

“Begin,” said the mayor, and dropped his silver handkerchief.

Caleb clamped his mouth shut. Seconds marched by in their polished boots. One minute. Two. The crowd counted in whispers, each number smaller than the last. At four minutes, Caleb’s face turned the color of plums and prophecy. At five, his eyes watered and the water rose from them in thin, obedient streams.

The scarecrow stood smiling with his stitched mouth.

At six minutes, Caleb’s knees trembled. Somewhere a jar of pickles burst. The church bell rang once by accident. Caleb opened his mouth and the breath leapt out, a pale horse, galloping over the pool’s cracked floor and away toward the county line.

Everyone turned to the scarecrow.

He had not breathed because he had never been asked to.

The crow declared him champion. The town applauded uncertainly, as people do when nature changes the subject. Caleb sat on the tiles, suddenly only a boy, his chest rising and falling like a porch screen in August.

That evening, they carried the scarecrow through the streets on their shoulders, though he weighed almost nothing, though he kept losing pieces of himself to the wind. Caleb walked behind him, holding the trophy, listening to the strange new music of his own breathing.

In the bean field, under a moon shaped like an open mouth, the champion was planted again.

By morning, every stalk had lungs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse narrative in the style of a contemporary American prose poem, featuring Kenji Takezo, a lucky twenty-pound brick, and a retired truck driver named Mack Stanton reading comics underwater.
counterfactuals.output:
Kenji Takezo found the twenty-pound brick behind the bowling alley, where the rain had written its brief autobiography in oil and gutter water. It was red, or had once been red, before weather and tires and the soft violence of years had worried it into the color of an old tongue. Kenji knew luck when he saw it. Luck was seldom gold. Luck was usually heavy, inconvenient, and waiting beside a dumpster.

He carried it home in both arms like a sleeping animal.

In town, nobody asked why Kenji Takezo kept a brick on the passenger seat of his car, buckled in with the good manners of a child. By then everyone had their own weather. The pharmacist was learning to whistle again after the divorce. The high school principal had begun wearing lavender socks. Mack Stanton, retired truck driver, had converted his backyard swimming pool into a library of impossible afternoons.

Mack had spent forty years hauling lettuce, machine parts, paperback mysteries, frozen turkeys, and once, by mistake, a crate of live bees from Fresno to Amarillo. Now he wore a diving mask and sank each morning to the bottom of the pool, where he sat in a lawn chair weighted with cinder blocks and read comics laminated page by page. Through the wavering blue, superheroes looked less certain of themselves. Their capes floated upward like questions. Speech bubbles trembled. Every POW! became a pearl of air.

Kenji visited on Thursdays. He placed the lucky brick at the pool’s edge and watched Mack descend with an issue of The Fantastic Four rolled under one arm. The old man’s silver hair lifted around his skull like smoke reconsidering the fire. Sometimes he laughed underwater, and the laughter climbed to the surface in bright, breakable coins.

Nobody knew what the brick was lucky for.

Then, one August afternoon, the sky went green as a bruise and the tornado sirens began their long animal moan. Kenji was at Mack’s house, holding a glass of iced tea, listening to the wind unzip the neighborhood. Mack was underwater, halfway through a battle between a woman made of light and a man who could not die. The lawn furniture rolled. The maples bent down as if ashamed. Kenji reached for the brick.

It did not save the house. It did not stop the storm. Luck is not a wall. Luck is a hand on your shoulder saying, Not that way.

Kenji dropped the brick into the pool.

It fell slow and solemn through the blue, turning once, twice, like a thought deciding where to land. Mack looked up from his comic. The brick struck the pool floor beside him with a dull, holy knock. He understood, or believed he did. He kicked upward, breaking the surface just as the sycamore came down where he had been sitting in the yard five minutes before, where he would have gone to fold the umbrella, where he would have stood muttering about weather like a man negotiating with God.

Afterward, the town smelled of splintered wood, wet insulation, and lilacs beaten flat. Kenji and Mack sat in the emptied bathtub with a flashlight between them, the lucky brick resting on Mack’s knees. Outside, alarms called to one another in the dark. Inside, Mack opened a damp comic and tried to read by the shaking light.

The panels had blurred. The hero’s face had run into the villain’s. The words were dissolving.

“Best issue yet,” Mack said.

Kenji nodded, because sometimes the story improves when it can no longer explain itself. The brick lay there, twenty pounds of ordinary earth fired hard enough to survive us, and nobody spoke for a while. They listened to the storm leaving town, dragging its chains behind it, and to the small, stubborn drip from the faucet—time, putting itself back together.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a deadpan, slightly absurd poem told from the perspective of townspeople watching their favorite local boy lose a swimming pool competition at twilight.
counterfactuals.output:
We gathered by the municipal pool  
with our folding chairs and moral support,  
which is similar to regular support  
but less useful in water.

Dusk arrived in its purple tracksuit.  
The lifeguard blew the whistle  
like a small train giving up.

There was our favorite local boy,  
Caleb, of the hardware store Calebs,  
adjusting his goggles  
with the seriousness of a man defusing a pie.

We had all expected victory.  
His mother had baked a sheet cake  
that said GOOD WORK, CALEB,  
which felt legally cautious.

The other swimmer was from out of town.  
He had shoulders like filing cabinets  
and entered the pool  
as if returning to his home planet.

At the signal they dove.  
Caleb made a noble splash.  
The out-of-town boy made no splash at all,  
which we found rude.

For a while Caleb was only slightly behind,  
then behind in the ordinary way,  
then behind in a historical sense.

We watched him kick and breathe,  
kick and breathe,  
like someone trying to explain bad news  
to a lake.

The sun lowered itself  
behind the concession stand.  
A moth landed on the scoreboard  
and stayed neutral.

When it ended, Caleb touched the wall  
second, which is a kind of touching the wall  
that no one puts on banners.

We clapped anyway.  
We are a community.  
We understand plumbing, weather,  
and the long civic labor of pretending.

Caleb climbed out, dripping and local.  
His father said, “Good effort,”  
in the tone usually reserved  
for casseroles with raisins.

The winner shook his hand.  
A cloud shaped like a receipt  
passed over the deep end.

Then we ate the cake.  
It tasted like frosting and revised expectations.  
Someone said the pool looked peaceful at twilight,  
and it did,  
except for the lanes,  
still holding their straight yellow opinions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic yet funny vignette about a boy whose only talents are surfing, troublemaking, and holding his breath, ending with him wanting to hear someone read to him.
counterfactuals.output:
By twelve, Milo had discovered he was good at exactly three things: surfing, troublemaking, and holding his breath.

Unfortunately, only one of these was considered a “marketable skill” by his teachers, and even then only if the market was underwater and poorly supervised.

He could stand on a board like he’d been born during a storm. He knew the moods of waves better than he knew multiplication. He could spot a good break from the school bus window and become so emotionally affected that he’d miss his stop, which he claimed was “a form of pilgrimage” and which his mother called “again, Milo?”

Troublemaking came naturally too. Not mean trouble. Not the sort that made smaller kids cry or windows expensive. Milo’s trouble was creative and usually damp. He once filled the principal’s umbrella with hermit crabs. He replaced the cafeteria’s motivational posters with hand-drawn warnings about sandwiches becoming sentient. He convinced half of Year Seven that the gym teacher had once been a dolphin but had lost a bet.

The breath-holding was less useful, though it impressed people at first.

“How long can you do it?” they’d ask.

Milo would shrug, inhale, and disappear beneath the surface of the municipal pool while everyone counted.

At one minute, they cheered.

At two, they got nervous.

At three, someone fetched an adult.

At four, Milo surfaced looking bored and a little blue, and the lifeguard banned him “emotionally, if not legally.”

His father used to say, “That boy could outlast a shipwreck,” and ruffle Milo’s hair with a hand that smelled of engine oil and salt. Then his father went out on a boat one winter morning and the sea, which had always seemed like Milo’s co-conspirator, turned quiet and kept him.

After that, people stopped laughing as much when Milo held his breath.

They watched him too closely. Teachers spoke to him in soft voices, which made him want to put frogs in their desk drawers. His mother hugged him like she was checking whether he was still there. Even the waves seemed to approach more carefully, folding themselves in gray and green, as if they had bad news but didn’t know how to say it.

So Milo surfed harder.

He paddled out before sunrise, when the beach was empty except for gulls, joggers, and old men with metal detectors searching for treasure in other people’s lost afternoons. He rode waves until his arms shook and his lips cracked white with salt. When he wiped out, he sank on purpose.

Down there, the world stopped asking questions.

No teachers. No casseroles from neighbors. No mother standing in the doorway at night pretending she had come to look for laundry. Just the deep hum of water and the thump of his own heart, stubborn as a fist on a locked door.

He could hold his breath long enough to imagine he had become something else.

A seal.

A stone.

A boy-shaped apology.

Then his lungs would burn, and he’d kick upward, bursting through the surface with a gasp so loud the gulls complained.

One afternoon, after getting suspended for arranging the school chairs into the shape of a giant squid—“symbolic,” he explained, though of what, he refused to say—Milo came home to find his mother asleep on the sofa with a book open on her chest.

She looked smaller asleep. Not weak, exactly. Just folded.

Milo stood there dripping seawater onto the rug, because he had stopped at the beach on the way home despite being specifically told not to stop at the beach on the way home. A thin line of kelp trailed from one ankle. In his pocket was a detention slip, three shells, and a dead crab he had forgotten about.

On the coffee table lay the book his mother had been reading. It was one his father used to read aloud in a pirate voice so bad it sounded Irish, Scottish, and concussed all at once.

Milo picked it up.

The pages smelled dusty and human. Someone had underlined a sentence in pencil. Probably his father. Probably years ago, when nobody knew anything yet.

His mother stirred. “Milo?”

He froze, as if caught robbing a bank instead of holding a paperback.

“You’re wet,” she said.

“I’m always a little wet,” he said.

“There’s a crab in your pocket, isn’t there?”

Milo considered lying, but the crab chose that moment to fall onto the floor with a dry, accusatory click.

His mother sighed. Then, unexpectedly, she laughed. It was a small laugh, rusty from disuse, but it made the room warmer.

Milo looked at the book in his hands.

Outside, the evening pressed its blue face to the windows. Somewhere far off, the sea dragged itself in and out, in and out, like something trying to breathe.

Milo climbed onto the sofa beside his mother, careful not to get too much saltwater on her sleeve.

“Can you,” he said, and stopped.

His mother waited.

He could hold his breath for four minutes and twenty-two seconds. He could ride a wave taller than a garage. He could get an entire assembly dismissed because of one strategically released chicken.

But he could not say the simple thing without feeling like he might sink.

So he held out the book.

“Can you read to me?” he asked.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a strange small-town story in lineated prose about an annual underwater breath-holding championship, with disappointment, comedy, and loneliness beneath the surface.
counterfactuals.output:
Every August, when the lake turned the color of old nickels,  
the town of Bellwether held its underwater breath-holding championship.

They called it The Long Silence.

A folding table was set up on the dock for registration,  
next to a cooler of orange slices, a church coffeepot,  
and the mayor’s laminated sign that read:

NO HORSEPLAY  
NO WISHING  
NO HOLDING BREATH TO PROVE A POINT

The last rule had been added after Mr. Pell  
stayed under for four minutes and came up divorced.

Nobody knew how that worked exactly,  
but his wife, Linda, had been seen standing on shore  
with her arms crossed so hard  
they seemed to have hinges.

The contestants were ordinary people, mostly.

There was Gary from the hardware store,  
who trained by refusing to answer customers.

There was Miss Emmaline, the retired second-grade teacher,  
who could sit perfectly still at the bottom of the lake  
with her cardigan floating around her like a jellyfish,  
and who had won twice before anyone realized  
she had been falling asleep.

There were the Flack twins, Kevin and Other Kevin,  
who entered every year in matching swim caps  
and always surfaced at the same time, furious,  
each accusing the other of cheating by existing.

And there was Nora Bell.

Nora worked nights at the 24-hour laundromat,  
where she watched strangers’ clothes go around  
and around in the blue-lit machines.

She had no husband, no dog, no emergency contact  
except the laundromat owner, who had once written her name  
on the wrong tax form and never corrected it.

She had practiced all summer in her bathtub.

She would fill it to the overflow drain,  
lower herself under,  
and listen to the pipes complain inside the walls.

At first she managed twenty seconds.

Then forty.

Then, one evening in July,  
while the ceiling fan turned like a slow accusation above her,  
she stayed under long enough  
to forget what she had meant to come up for.

This seemed promising.

On championship morning, the whole town gathered.

Children sat on towels eating powdered donuts.  
Teenagers pretended they had not come to watch.  
Old men in seed caps discussed lung capacity  
as if it were a kind of weather.

The lake lay flat and green,  
with only the cattails moving,  
whispering among themselves like they had heard things.

Mayor Wexley stood on the dock in his ceremonial sash,  
which was just the Christmas parade sash turned inside out.

“Citizens,” he said into a bullhorn that squealed  
as if personally offended,  
“today we honor the proud Bellwether tradition  
of going down into the water  
and not making a fuss about it.”

Everyone clapped.

A goose also clapped, somehow.

The contestants lined up at the edge.

Nora looked down.

Beneath the dock, minnows flashed like small ideas.  
Somewhere below them, in the cool brown dimness,  
were beer cans, lost sunglasses,  
the mayor’s first wedding ring,  
and the rusted bicycle everyone claimed belonged  
to a boy who had moved away,  
though no one could remember his name.

“Ready,” called the referee, Mrs. Bunt,  
who sold insurance and carried a stopwatch  
with the authority of a judge.

The contestants inhaled.

The whole town inhaled with them.

For one brief second, Bellwether lifted itself up  
by the lungs.

Then the whistle blew.

They went under.

At first there was comedy.

Other Kevin immediately kicked Kevin in the face.

Gary from the hardware store drifted sideways  
with his arms folded,  
looking exactly like he did  
when someone asked where the masonry screws were.

Miss Emmaline descended serenely,  
eyes closed,  
as if punishing the lake with quiet time.

Nora sank.

The water received her without comment.

Sound vanished, or changed shape.  
Above her, the crowd became a trembling gray quilt.  
Legs dangled. Bubbles rose from mouths,  
small confessions escaping too early.

Nora held still.

She thought of the laundromat at 3:00 a.m.,  
of the vending machine that sold only pretzels  
and one ancient packet of peanut butter crackers  
no one ever bought.

She thought of couples folding sheets together,  
snapping them open between their bodies  
like sails.

She thought of how people said her name  
only when they needed quarters.

Around her, the competition thinned.

Gary surfaced first, gasping,  
then claimed he had swallowed a fish  
“of considerable size.”

The Flack twins burst up together,  
shouting through coughs.

“He blinked at me!”

“I was drowning, Kevin!”

“Exactly!”

Miss Emmaline remained below, smiling faintly,  
until Mrs. Bunt tapped her with the rescue pole  
and she rose, annoyed,  
muttering about indoor voices.

Now only Nora and a boy named Timmy Starch remained.

Timmy was seventeen and famous  
for having once eaten a decorative candle  
during the Founders’ Day banquet.

He had entered on a dare  
and was underwater with the wide-eyed terror  
of someone who had just remembered mortality.

Nora could see him across the murk,  
his cheeks puffed,  
his limbs jerking in small negotiations.

Above, the crowd noticed.

The dock thundered with feet.

“Nora!” someone shouted, or maybe “More of ’er!”  
Sound did strange things through water.

Timmy’s eyes met hers.

He pointed up.

Nora nodded, or thought she did.

Timmy shot to the surface  
with the graceless urgency of a cork.

The town exploded.

Nora was alone in the lake.

This was the moment she had wanted,  
though wanting it now seemed embarrassing.

At the bottom, weeds brushed her ankles  
with the intimacy of strangers on a bus.

Her lungs burned.

Still she stayed.

She pictured coming up triumphant.  
The mayor shaking her wet hand.  
Her photograph in the Bellwether Bulletin:  
LOCAL WOMAN DOES NOT BREATHE FOR TOWN RECORD.

Maybe people would wave at her after that.  
Maybe someone would ask  
what she did besides laundry.

Maybe the world above the water  
would have rearranged itself slightly  
in her favor.

Her chest tightened.

The lake darkened around the edges.

Then, below her, something moved.

Not a fish.

Not exactly.

A shape in the silt, long and pale,  
opened what might have been an eye.

Nora stared.

The thing stared back with the exhausted patience  
of something that had been waiting years  
for anyone to visit and mean it.

It lifted a hand.

Or a root.

Or the handlebar of the old bicycle.

Nora panicked and laughed at the same time,  
which underwater is a poor strategy.

Bubbles burst from her nose.

She kicked upward.

She rose too fast, arms windmilling,  
hair streaming behind her like black pondweed,  
and broke the surface with a sound  
half gasp, half honk.

The crowd cheered.

Then hesitated.

Mrs. Bunt checked the stopwatch.

Mayor Wexley leaned in.

“Three minutes and twelve seconds,” she announced.

A murmur passed over Bellwether.

The record was three minutes and thirteen.

Set by Mr. Pell the year of the divorce.

Nora clung to the ladder, coughing lake water,  
while everyone made the same face:  
the face people make when they are prepared to celebrate  
but must return the celebration to its box.

“Still very good,” said the mayor.

“Very, very good,” said Mrs. Bunt.

“Practically winning,” said Linda Pell,  
who had appeared from nowhere  
with a cigarette and a folding chair.

Timmy Starch was declared champion by default,  
because he was technically the last person  
to surface before Nora,  
and also because no one understood the rules.

He received the trophy,  
a silver-plated diver mounted on a wooden base,  
whose tiny engraved plaque had room  
for only one more name.

Timmy held it upside down  
and vomited into a bush.

Everyone agreed this was youthful exuberance.

Nora sat on the dock wrapped in a beach towel  
printed with cartoon lobsters.

Water streamed from her hair into her eyes.  
Someone handed her an orange slice.  
Someone else said, “You’ll get it next year,”  
which is the kind of kindness  
that already has its coat on.

The crowd loosened and drifted away.

The Flack twins argued beside the hot dog stand.

Miss Emmaline asked if the lake had homework.

Gary told three children about the enormous fish  
that had entered him “with intent.”

By late afternoon, the dock was nearly empty.

Nora remained.

Her clothes stuck to her skin.  
The lake had gone quiet again,  
the way rooms go quiet after company leaves  
and the furniture admits what it has endured.

Mayor Wexley came by to collect the sign.

“Fine effort,” he said.

“Thank you,” Nora said.

“Shame about the second.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the water.

“People don’t realize,” he said,  
“how long a second can be.”

Then he carried the sign away.

Nora watched the place where she had come up.

She thought about the pale shape below,  
the eye, the hand, the invitation or warning.

Probably it had been a branch.

Probably it had been fear  
wearing a local costume.

Across the lake, the first porch lights blinked on,  
one by one,  
small domestic stars belonging to other people.

Nora stood and squeezed water from her hair.

At the laundromat that night,  
someone had left a load in dryer number six.

Men’s shirts, a child’s pajamas,  
one red sock.

She folded them carefully.

At 2:17 a.m., no one came.

The machines hummed around her  
like distant applause.

Nora sat on the counter,  
took a breath,  
and held it.

Not for the town.

Not for the trophy.

Not even for next year.

She held it to feel, for a few seconds,  
the shape of the silence inside her.

It was larger than she remembered.

It had weeds in it.

It had orange slices, and old bicycles,  
and a boy vomiting victory into a bush.

It had a pale thing at the bottom  
that might someday speak.

When she finally exhaled,  
the laundromat windows fogged softly,  
as if the whole building had breathed with her  
and been disappointed too.
